When will I use this?

Gradients: when will I use this?

Whenever something slopes and you need to say how steeply.

Highways engineer

Construction and the built environment

\(\displaystyle \text{gradient} = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}\)

How far does a 10% hill climb in a kilometre?

A steep-hill sign shows the gradient as a percentage: 10% is 1 in 10 (1 m up for every 10 m along).

  1. Over 1 km at 10%: \(1000 \times 0.10 = 100\) m of height.
  2. 20% is \(1 \div 0.2 = 1\) in 5, twice as steep.

The answer: \(1000 \times 0.10 = 100\) m climb

Architectural technician

Construction and the built environment

\(\displaystyle \text{rise} \le \dfrac{\text{length}}{12}\)

How high can a 2 m wheelchair ramp rise?

Building regulations set how steep a wheelchair ramp may be. The shorter the ramp, the steeper it is allowed: \(1 : 12\) for a 2 m ramp, \(1 : 20\) for 10 m.

  1. 2 m ramp: \(2000 \div 12 = 166.7\) mm, so the rise can be at most 166 mm (round down: it's a maximum).
  2. 10 m ramp: \(10000 \div 20 = 500\) mm.

The answer: \(2000 \div 12 = 166.7\) mm

Practise it

Games on MaffsGames that practise gradients:

  • Gradient Hunter: Find the gradient of real-world graphs and say what the rate of change means.
  • Coordinate Geometry Dash: Midpoints, gradients, lengths and equations of lines and circles on a plotted grid.
  • Core Maths Paper 2C Practice: Exam-style questions for AQA Core Maths Paper 2C: graphs, rates of change and exponential models.
